title: Seeing beneath the surface
summary: Raking light, ultraviolet, infrared and X-rays: what each reveals, and how to read them on the case-file portrait.

shots.title:
Seeing beneath
the surface.
shots.subtitle: Raking light, ultraviolet, infrared, X-ray.
shots.narration: Before anyone takes a sample, examiners look — with light the eye can't use on its own. Each kind of light answers a different question about the layers.
Raking light skims the surface from one side, throwing every crack, ridge of impasto and lifting flake into relief. On our case file the cracks look suspiciously sharp and regular.

shots.text: Old varnish **glows greenish-yellow**. Paint on top of it **reads dark**.
shots.narration: Under ultraviolet, traditional resin varnishes glow a greenish yellow. Anything painted on top of that varnish — a retouching, or a convenient signature — blocks the glow and reads dark.
On the case-file portrait, the varnish glows evenly — but the signature sits on top of it, dark. It was added after the picture had been varnished.

shots.text: Infrared passes through paint. **Carbon black** stops it.
shots.narration: Infrared passes through most paint until something absorbs it. Carbon black absorbs strongly, so a black underdrawing on a white ground shows up in an infrared image.
Here the underdrawing appears, and the hand was first drawn lower, then moved: a pentimento. That suggests an original composition rather than a copy — but it is not proof.

shots.text: Heavy atoms block X-rays: **lead white** shows bright.
shots.narration: X-rays pass through light materials but are blocked by heavy atoms. Lead, atomic number 82, makes lead white show bright; nails show too, and every layer appears at once.
The X-ray of our panel shows the lead-white cap and ruff — and, underneath, a horizon and trees. The portrait was painted over an older picture.

shots.text: X-ray and UV entered authentication in the **1930s**.
shots.narration: These tools aren't new: X-ray and ultraviolet photography, with chemical analysis of pigments, entered art authentication in the 1930s. What's new is resolution, and combining methods.

steps.title: Watch: Van Eyck's drawing under the paint
steps.caption: The National Gallery shows Jan van Eyck's original drawing beneath 'The Arnolfini Portrait', revealed by infrared imaging.

steps.title: The examination bench
steps.brief: This is the case-file portrait you will judge in your capstone. Switch light sources and inspect each region. Log every finding — some point to a fake, one is normal for an old painting, and one points the other way. Then save the results to your casebook.

items.title: Sharp, regular cracks
items.finding: The crack network is crisp and evenly spaced, with straight segments, like shallow grooves.
items.hint: Does the surface age the way old paint does?
items.why: Real craquelure forms as layers age and shrink; a 3D study found forged cracks shaped as simple V-grooves rather than deep, square-sided breaks.

items.title: Even greenish glow
items.finding: The varnish fluoresces an even greenish yellow across the background.
items.why: Aged natural-resin varnishes glow greenish yellow under UV — normal for an old, varnished picture. (A forger can varnish too.)

items.title: Signature on top of the varnish
items.finding: The signature and date read dark against the glowing varnish.
items.hint: Is the signature as old as the paint around it?
items.why: Paint applied over the varnish blocks the UV and shows dark, so the signature was added after the picture was varnished.

items.title: A moved hand (pentimento)
items.finding: The underdrawing shows the hand first sketched lower, then shifted up.
items.hint: Did the painter change their mind anywhere?
items.why: Pentimenti record a composition being worked out — typical of an original rather than a copy, though a forger can change his mind too.

items.title: Another picture underneath
items.finding: A horizon, trees and a lead-white sky lie beneath the portrait.
items.why: Reused supports are a classic forger's tactic: an old panel dates correctly while the new paint does not. Artists reused panels too, so the paint itself must be dated.

steps.title: Go deeper: 'The Girl in the Spotlight'
steps.caption: The Mauritshuis documents its research project on Vermeer's 'Girl with a Pearl Earring' — what a modern technical examination of a masterpiece looks like.

questions.prompt: Under UV, a signature reads dark against glowing varnish. What does that suggest?
options: It is the oldest part of the painting
It was painted after the varnish was applied
It is written in lead white
questions.explain: Paint on top of the varnish blocks the fluorescence.

options: It passes through paint, and carbon black absorbs it
questions.explain: A black drawing on a white ground contrasts strongly in infrared.

questions.prompt: Why does lead white appear bright in an X-radiograph?
questions.explain: The heavier the atoms, the more they impede X-rays.

questions.prompt: An X-ray shows a different picture underneath. What follows?
options: The support was reused — common in forgeries, but artists did it too; date the paint
